title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #21 (Exam-Style Tier)
description: Full-length 53-question simulation in the applied-scenario style (120 minutes): constraint-driven scenarios, code and config snippets, and short options that are all real features but only one fits.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)

options.text: It never handles `canceled` and `expired` results, so those requests are dropped without a trace
It requeues errored requests unchanged, but `invalid_request_error` means the body needs fixing first
It should shrink each nightly batch below the 256 MB size limit to stop these errors
It should read the batch's `request_counts` to decide which records to resend in the next nightly batch

questions.explanation: An `errored` result covers two different situations. When the error type is `invalid_request_error`, the request body itself is wrong, so it must be corrected before it is sent again. Other error types, such as a server error, can simply be retried. A handler that requeues everything keeps replaying the same bad bodies. Analogy: a parcel returned because the address is wrong. Dropping it back in the mailbox unchanged just brings it back next week, so you correct the address first, whereas a parcel delayed by a truck breakdown can simply be sent again. Missing handling for canceled and expired results is a genuine gap, but those are different result types from the one failing here.

distractor_explanations.A: That gap is real, but it is not what the stem shows. The failing records are `errored` results carrying `invalid_request_error`, not canceled or expired ones.
distractor_explanations.C: Size limits apply to the batch as a whole and can show up as a 413 `request_too_large` at submission. They do not produce per-record errored results for a small share of requests.
distractor_explanations.D: `request_counts` holds only totals for the four result states. It cannot say which records failed or why, while the per-request `custom_id` and error type can.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A support assistant sends two `document` blocks in one Messages request: a 60-page policy PDF whose answers must show page-level citations, and a short plain-text style guide that should only shape tone. Citations are enabled on the PDF alone. The team wants to keep one request on the first-party API. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add a `context` string to the style guide stating that Claude must never cite it
Enable `citations` on the style guide too, so the whole request carries one common setting
Convert the style guide into a PDF, giving both documents the same citation format
Split the work into two requests, one per document, and merge the two answers afterwards

questions.explanation: Citations are all-or-none across the documents in a single request: either every document block has `citations.enabled` set to true or none does. Documents that were only meant to guide tone can still be included with citations on, and Claude simply cites what it draws from. Analogy: a group chat where read receipts are on for everyone or off for everyone. You cannot switch them on for one friend only, so you either accept receipts from all or give up on them. A `context` note works like a sticky note on one message, which Claude reads but which does not change the chat setting.

distractor_explanations.A: `context` is passed to the model as background and is not used toward cited content. It is not a switch that turns citations off for one document.
distractor_explanations.C: The rule concerns the `enabled` flag, not the document type, so a PDF would not change the all-or-none requirement.
distractor_explanations.D: That would avoid the mixed setting, but it breaks the stated wish to keep one request and loses Claude's ability to answer across both documents.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: An overnight analytics job builds a Message Batch whose `custom_id` values are customer email addresses. Creation is rejected, and the error message points at `custom_id`. The job needs to map every result back to its source record, and it runs overnight at the batch discount with no one waiting. Which change fits best?

options.text: Use an opaque ID like `rec_48213` as `custom_id` and keep a lookup table to the record
Omit `custom_id` and match each result to its request by its position in the results file
Submit one batch per customer, which removes the need for a per-request identifier
Switch the job to synchronous `messages.create` calls and drop the identifiers entirely

questions.explanation: A `custom_id` must be 1 to 64 characters long and contain only letters, digits, hyphens and underscores, so an email address with `@` and dots is rejected. Because results return in any order, the ID is the only reliable join key, so use a short opaque value and keep the mapping to the real record in your own store. This also keeps email addresses out of the batch request itself.

distractor_explanations.B: `custom_id` is a required field, and results can come back in any order, so position in the file says nothing about which request produced a result.
distractor_explanations.C: Every request in a batch still needs a `custom_id`. One batch per customer also multiplies the calls that count against the batch rate limits.
distractor_explanations.D: That removes the problem but gives up the 50% batch discount. The job is overnight work with no user waiting, which is what batches are for.

options.text: Remove the range and length keywords, keep the types, and check the limits in your own code
Keep the schema unchanged and state both limits in the prompt text for Claude to follow
Declare `score` as an `enum` of the values 1 to 5 and leave the `maxLength` on `summary` in place
Set `additionalProperties` to `true` so the schema may carry keywords the compiler ignores

questions.explanation: Structured outputs accept only part of JSON Schema. Numeric limits such as `minimum` and `maximum`, string limits such as `minLength` and `maxLength`, and `additionalProperties` other than `false` make the API return a 400. Keep the shape in the schema and check the value ranges yourself after parsing. SDK helpers do the same trick for you by stripping the keywords, noting them in the description, and validating locally. Analogy: a vending machine that only accepts certain coins. It cannot check that you paid exactly right for the combo deal, so the cashier at the exit counts the change. Declaring an enum fixes only half of the schema here.

distractor_explanations.B: The unsupported keywords are still in the schema, so the 400 remains. Moving the limits into the prompt only helps after the schema itself is fixed.
distractor_explanations.C: An `enum` would cover the score, but the `maxLength` on `summary` is still an unsupported keyword, so the request keeps failing with a 400.
distractor_explanations.D: `additionalProperties` must be `false` for objects. The compiler does not ignore unsupported keywords; it rejects the schema with a 400.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A contract-review service sends `document` blocks with citations enabled, and its UI links each claim to a PDF page. The team now adds `output_config.format` with a JSON schema so a parser receives typed fields, and every call returns HTTP 400. Only the first-party Messages API is approved. What is the best fix?

options.text: Drop `output_config.format`, keep citations on, and validate the reply's shape in your own code
Keep both, but upload the PDFs through the Files API and reference them by `file_id`
Disable citations and have Claude quote the passage and page number inside the JSON fields
Send the structured call to a Bedrock-hosted model and the citations call to the first-party API

questions.explanation: Citations and structured outputs cannot be combined: if a user-provided document or search result has citations enabled and `output_config.format` is also set, the API returns a 400. Citations need citation blocks interleaved with the text, which strict JSON schema output does not allow. When the UI truly needs citations, keep them and check the reply's shape in your own code. Analogy: a form with fixed boxes versus a report with footnotes. Footnotes cannot live inside the boxes, so you cannot have both on the same page. Moving the files elsewhere does not change the page layout rule.

distractor_explanations.B: A `file_id` document supports citations like any other source. The conflict is between citations and structured outputs, whatever the document source.
distractor_explanations.C: That gives typed fields, but the page numbers would be model-written text. The UI needs the API-parsed pointers that citations guarantee.
distractor_explanations.D: This uses a second platform that security has not approved, and it leaves two separate answers that still have to be merged.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A knowledge-base tool returns the block below, and the next request is rejected with a validation error. The app wants Claude to cite the article and also to know how many articles matched.

```json
{
  "type": "tool_result",
  "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A",
  "content": [
    {"type": "text", "text": "1 article matched."},
    {"type": "search_result",
     "source": "kb://refunds",
     "title": "Refund policy",
     "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Refunds take 14 days."}],
     "citations": {"enabled": true}}
  ]
}
```

Which change fixes it with the least rework?

options.text: Add `cache_control: {"type": "ephemeral"}` to the `search_result` block to make the combination valid
Remove the leading text block and put the match count in the `search_result`'s own `content` array
Change `source` to a public https URL instead of the internal `kb://` identifier
Set `citations.enabled` to `false` and let Claude quote the article from plain text

questions.explanation: Inside a `tool_result`, if any block is a `search_result` then every block must be one; mixing in a plain text block triggers a validation error. Supporting text belongs inside one of the search results' own `content` arrays, where it also becomes citable. Analogy: a mail slot labelled for parcels only or letters only. If you shove a letter in with the parcels, the whole delivery bounces, so you tuck the note inside the parcel instead. A different address format would not matter, and a sticker for reuse, the cache setting, does nothing about what the slot accepts.

distractor_explanations.A: `cache_control` is a real option on search results, used for reuse across requests. It has no effect on the rule about mixing block types.
distractor_explanations.C: `source` accepts any stable string, including internal identifiers. The rejection comes from mixing a text block with a search result in one tool result.
distractor_explanations.D: Tool results can carry cited search results, so this gives up the stated citation need and still leaves the mixed block types in place.

questions.prompt: A meeting-notes assistant stores each transcript as a list of speaker turns and must cite whole turns. With plain text documents, citations point at sentence fragments inside a turn. The request uses the same Messages API with citations enabled. Which change fits best?

options.text: Send the transcripts as PDF documents so citations are anchored to page numbers
Send each transcript as a custom content document with one content block per speaker turn
Add a `context` string to each document describing the turn boundaries for Claude to respect
Raise `max_tokens` so Claude has room to quote complete turns in its answer

questions.explanation: Plain text and PDF documents are automatically split into sentences, and those are the smallest units Claude can cite. A custom content document is used as supplied, with no further chunking, and its citations refer to your content blocks by index. Putting one block per speaker turn makes each turn the citable unit. Analogy: a pizza. By default the shop cuts it into small slices, and you can only hand over slices. If you want each guest's portion to stay whole, you arrange the pre-cut portions yourself. Telling the shop about portion sizes in a note does not change how it slices.

distractor_explanations.A: PDF text is chunked into sentences just like plain text, and citations carry page ranges. Neither gives turn-level units.
distractor_explanations.C: `title` and `context` go to the model but are not used toward cited content. The chunking of the document stays the same.
distractor_explanations.D: Chunk granularity is set by the document type, and `cited_text` is not counted toward output tokens, so `max_tokens` plays no part.

options.text: It should add an `input_json_delta` branch and parse the fragments once the block stops
It should read a final `citations` list from the `message_stop` event once all text has arrived
It indexes `blocks` by `ev.index`, but citations are keyed by `document_index`, so the lookup misses
It ignores `citations_delta` events, each of which carries one citation to add to that text block

questions.explanation: With streaming, each citation arrives as a `citations_delta` inside a `content_block_delta` event, and each delta holds one citation to push onto the `citations` list of the current text block. A loop that handles only `text_delta` therefore rebuilds the text but silently drops every citation. Analogy: a live TV broadcast that has a captions channel alongside the audio. If you only record the audio track, the words are all there but the on-screen source labels never make it to your copy. Waiting for the end of the show does not help, because the labels were never saved.

distractor_explanations.A: That delta type streams the input of `tool_use` blocks. Citations use their own delta type inside the same `content_block_delta` event.
distractor_explanations.B: `message_stop` carries no payload. Citations arrive as deltas on the text block while the answer streams.
distractor_explanations.C: `ev.index` is the position of the content block, which is the right key for text. `document_index` sits inside each citation and names the source document.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A gateway routes each request to the cheapest model that accepts PDF input and supports structured outputs. Its routing table is hand-edited after each model launch and has twice sent PDFs to models that rejected them. The first-party API is the only approved platform. What should replace the table?

options.text: Use `max_input_tokens` from the Models API response as the signal for PDF and structured-output support
Query `GET /v1/models` on a schedule and filter models on their `capabilities` flags before routing
Infer support from the date in each model `id` and assume newer snapshots accept PDFs
Send each request to the cheapest model and retry on the next one after any HTTP 400

questions.explanation: The Models API lists available models and, for each one, a `capabilities` object with flags such as `pdf_input`, `structured_outputs`, `batch` and `citations`, plus fields like `max_input_tokens`. A router that reads those flags stays correct when new models arrive, with no hand-edited table. Analogy: asking the restaurant for today's menu instead of relying on a photocopy from last season. The copy still lists dishes the kitchen stopped making, while a fresh menu always matches what can be ordered. Guessing from the dish name, the model ID, is worse than reading the menu.

distractor_explanations.A: That field gives the context window size. Support for PDFs and structured outputs sits in the `pdf_input` and `structured_outputs` capability entries.
distractor_explanations.C: A model ID is not a capability signal, and IDs of recent models do not even carry a date. The Models API reports capabilities directly.
distractor_explanations.D: Each rejection costs a round trip, and a 400 can come from a bad request body rather than from missing support, so the retry hides real errors.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A model the organization depends on is marked deprecated with a retirement date. About 30 services and CI jobs share a handful of API keys, and nobody can say which of them still call that model. Which first step finds them most reliably?

options.text: Search every repository for the model name and treat the matches as the complete list of callers
Export the Console Usage page as CSV and review every API key's usage broken down by model
Wait for the retirement date, then fix whichever services start to fail in production
Replace each pinned model ID with an alias in the services before measuring their usage

questions.explanation: Anthropic documents a simple audit: on the Usage page in the Console, export the data as CSV and review the breakdown by API key and model. That shows which keys still send traffic to the deprecated model, so teams can be contacted and migrated before the retirement date. Searching code only finds references that appear in code, and waiting means finding out through failures.

distractor_explanations.A: Model names often come from environment variables, config services or aliases that a text search misses. Usage data shows what is actually being called.
distractor_explanations.C: Requests to a retired model fail, so this turns the discovery step into a production outage.
distractor_explanations.D: Moving to aliases is not discovery, and it lets future upstream model changes land without anyone tracking them.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A gateway calls the token-counting endpoint before every request to enforce a per-user budget. At peak, count calls return HTTP 429 while `messages.create` calls on the same key still succeed. Only the first-party API is approved. Which explanation and response fit best?

options.text: Token counting is billed per call, so the account has reached a spend limit and needs it raised
Cache the count responses with a `cache_control` breakpoint so repeated counts stop hitting the limit
Counting shares the input-token budget with `messages.create`, so lower `max_tokens` on the real calls
Counting has its own per-minute limit by tier; count only large prompts or ask for a higher limit

questions.explanation: The token-counting endpoint is free, but it is limited by requests per minute according to your usage tier, and that limit is independent of the limits on creating messages. A gateway that counts every request can exhaust the counting limit while real calls still flow. Counting only prompts near the budget, or requesting a higher limit, addresses the cause. Counting spend is not the issue, because the endpoint costs nothing.

distractor_explanations.A: Counting is free to use. A spend cap would also block `messages.create`, which the stem says still succeeds.
distractor_explanations.B: Counting does not use prompt caching; `cache_control` blocks are accepted but only act during real message creation.
distractor_explanations.C: Token counting and message creation have separate, independent rate limits, and `max_tokens` affects output rather than the counting endpoint.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A team puts `cache_control` on a 40k-token system block, then sends the same body to the token-counting endpoint to learn how many tokens a repeat call will bill at the cache-read rate. The response shows one `input_tokens` number for the whole prompt. Which reading is right, and what should they do?

options.text: Counting applies no caching, so read `cache_read_input_tokens` from `usage` on real responses
Remove `cache_control` from the counting body, which the endpoint rejects
The number already excludes the cached block, so it shows only the part billed at the full rate
Call counting twice with the same body so the second call reads the cache and reports the split

questions.explanation: The token-counting endpoint returns an estimate of total input tokens and does not run caching logic, even if the body carries `cache_control` blocks. To see how much of a real request was read from or written to the cache, inspect `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` in the `usage` of an actual response. Analogy: a shop's price estimator on the wall quotes the full shelf price, while only the receipt at checkout shows the coupons that were applied. Asking the estimator twice never produces a coupon. It also does not complain when you hold up a coupon, it just ignores it.

distractor_explanations.B: The endpoint accepts `cache_control` blocks. It simply does not act on them, so removing them changes nothing about the count.
distractor_explanations.C: Counting is an estimate of the whole prompt without any caching logic. It does not subtract cached content.
distractor_explanations.D: Prompt caching happens only during real message creation. Repeating a count never creates or reads a cache entry.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A classifier uses `output_config.format` and declares `category` as an `enum` of three strings. About 1% of replies fail this check, yet each response completes with `stop_reason: end_turn`. Failing values look like `"Billing issue"`.

```python
ALLOWED = {"Billing Issue", "Account Access", "Feature Request"}
data = json.loads(resp.content[0].text)
if data["category"] not in ALLOWED:
    raise ValueError("bad category")
```

What explains this, and what is the best fix?

options.text: A refusal produced the mismatch, so check for `stop_reason: refusal` and retry the call
Enum casing is not guaranteed, so compare case-insensitively or normalise before checking
The 24-hour grammar cache was evicted, so the output ran unconstrained; resubmit the schema
The reply hit `max_tokens` mid-value, so raise the limit to stop the truncated strings

questions.explanation: Structured outputs guarantee the shape of the JSON, but not the capitalization of string `enum` and `const` values: Claude may return a value that differs from the schema only in case, typically the first letter of a word after a space. The response still finishes normally, with no error and no special stop reason. The fix is to compare case-insensitively, and to avoid enum values that differ only by capitalization. Analogy: a librarian looking up a book title on a form. Searching the catalogue ignoring capital letters finds the book every time, whereas demanding identical capitals rejects good matches. The cache, refusals and truncation each leave their own clues, none of which appear here.

distractor_explanations.A: A refusal is reported through its own stop reason. The stem shows `end_turn` on every failing response.
distractor_explanations.C: The grammar cache affects first-request latency, not correctness, and the replies are well-formed enum-like strings that differ only in case.
distractor_explanations.D: A truncated reply would carry `stop_reason: max_tokens` and cut-off text. `"Billing issue"` is a complete value with different capitalization.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A report job creates a batch of 50,000 requests on the first-party API and immediately tries to download from `results_url`, which is `null`. The developer adds a polling loop and needs a stopping rule that always works. Which rule is correct?

options.text: Poll until `processing_status` is `ended`, then stream the file at `results_url`
Poll until `request_counts.errored` is zero, then download the finished results
Wait until the `expires_at` time passes, then download whatever results are available
Sleep for 60 minutes and then download; batches are always finished within one hour

questions.explanation: A batch starts as `in_progress` and moves to `ended` once every request has finished. Only then are the results complete and available at `results_url`, which is `null` until that point. Polling `processing_status` is therefore the dependable stopping rule. A partial count or a fixed sleep guesses at the finish time.

distractor_explanations.B: The per-state counts stay at zero until the whole batch has ended, so a zero `errored` count is true from the first poll. Only `processing_status` signals completion.
distractor_explanations.C: `expires_at` is the 24-hour deadline. Waiting for it wastes hours when the batch ends earlier, and an expired request has no result to download.
distractor_explanations.D: Most batches finish within an hour, but a batch can take up to 24 hours and may expire.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A privacy review finds that a batch still in progress was built from the wrong data extract. The team wants the batch and its stored requests removed as soon as possible. The batch lives on the first-party API. What is the correct sequence?

options.text: Call the delete endpoint straight away; it cancels in-progress batches before removing them
Archive the workspace that owns the batch, which removes its batches immediately
Cancel the batch, wait for it to end, then call `DELETE /v1/messages/batches/{batch_id}`
Wait for the 29-day retention window to lapse, as stored batches cannot be deleted sooner

questions.explanation: Batch requests and results are stored for up to 29 days, but you can delete a batch whenever processing has finished with `DELETE /v1/messages/batches/{batch_id}`. A batch that is still running must be canceled first; it moves through `canceling` to `ended`, and then the delete call works. Analogy: a print queue. You stop the job that is still printing before you can delete the file, and shredding the whole office printer to get rid of one job would be far too drastic.

distractor_explanations.A: An in-progress batch has to be canceled first. The delete call is meant for batches whose processing has finished.
distractor_explanations.B: Archiving a workspace cannot be undone and archives every API key created for it. It is not the documented way to remove one batch.
distractor_explanations.D: A batch can be deleted at any time after processing. The 29 days is how long results stay downloadable and data is stored.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt:
A team moves a nightly job from synchronous calls to Message Batches on the first-party API. Each request is built like this:

```python
client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=4096,
    stream=True,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
    tools=[WEB_SEARCH_TOOL],
    messages=msgs,
)
```

Which TWO statements are correct for the batch version? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `thinking` must be dropped, as batch requests cannot use extended or adaptive thinking
The `web_search` server tool can stay, and the batch worker runs the same server-side loop
`stream=True` must be removed, as batch results arrive in a single results file
The 50% discount covers only input tokens, and output tokens are billed at the standard rate
A `custom_id` may repeat across requests, provided the `messages` differ

questions.explanation: A few Messages parameters are not accepted in batch requests, and `stream: true` is one of them because batch results come back as a single results file rather than a stream. Almost everything else carries over, including extended thinking and all server tools, since the batch worker runs the same server-side agentic loop. All usage is billed at half price, and every request needs a unique `custom_id`. Analogy: moving house. The sofa and the boxes go in the truck, but the live phone call to your friend cannot be packed. The things that need an open line are what stay behind, and the rest of your belongings travel as normal.

distractor_explanations.A: Extended thinking is among the features that can be batched. Only a small set of parameters, such as `stream`, is rejected.
distractor_explanations.D: The batch discount applies to all usage: input tokens, output tokens and special tokens alike.
distractor_explanations.E: Each request in a batch needs its own unique `custom_id`, because results are matched to requests through it.

questions.topic: Moving a Call into a Batch

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A RAG backend returns `search_result` blocks, some inside tool results and some as top-level user content. Which TWO statements describe how those blocks behave? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The `content` array may mix text and image blocks, and Claude can cite either kind
They may appear in user messages and tool results, but an assistant message holding one is rejected
Citations default to off, and all `search_result` blocks in a request must match on `enabled`
A `search_result` block that carries `cache_control` is rejected by the Messages API
`cited_text` is counted toward output tokens, so quoting long passages makes each response costlier

questions.explanation: Search result blocks come with a few firm rules. Citations are disabled unless you set `citations.enabled`, and the setting is all-or-nothing: mixed settings in one request cause an error. The blocks belong in user messages, including inside tool results, and an assistant message that contains one is rejected. Analogy: a school trip form. Either every student's slip has the photo-permission box ticked or none does, and only parents, the user side, may hand slips in; a slip from a teacher, the assistant side, is turned away. Laminating a slip, the cache setting, is welcome, and quoting its words costs nothing extra.

distractor_explanations.A: Search results hold text only, so images and other media are not supported inside the `content` array.
distractor_explanations.D: `cache_control` is supported on search results and lets them be cached for reuse across requests.
distractor_explanations.E: `cited_text` is provided for convenience and does not count toward output tokens.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A platform team writes its model-retirement runbook from Anthropic's lifecycle documentation for the first-party API. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud follow the same retirement dates as the first-party API
Customers with active deployments get at least 60 days' notice before a public model retires
A deprecated model keeps working until its retirement date, and a replacement is named
A model listed as Legacy already has a fixed retirement date and stops working on it
Requests to a retired model are routed to the recommended replacement with no code change needed

questions.explanation: Anthropic describes four lifecycle states. Active models are fully supported; Legacy models no longer receive updates and may be deprecated later; Deprecated models still function but come with a recommended replacement and a retirement date; Retired models fail. For publicly released models, customers with active deployments are told at least 60 days ahead. Analogy: an airline schedule change. Your old flight still flies until the announced date and you are offered a replacement flight, but on the day after, the old flight simply does not exist and nobody rebooks you automatically. A different airline, the partner cloud, runs its own timetable.

distractor_explanations.A: Partner-operated platforms set their own retirement schedules, so lifecycle status and dates can differ there.
distractor_explanations.D: Legacy means the model gets no more updates and may be deprecated later. The retirement date is assigned at the Deprecated stage.
distractor_explanations.E: Requests to a retired model fail. Migrating to the replacement is the customer's job, done before the retirement date.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A gateway sends a 3,000-token shared prefix of tool definitions and system prompt, with one `cache_control` breakpoint on the last system block. Simple turns go to Claude Sonnet 5.5 and escalations go to Claude Haiku 4.5. The team compares the usage blocks of each model after an hour of steady traffic. What do they see?

options.text: Both models show a write, then reads, with the two tiers sharing one entry for the prefix.
Sonnet 5.5 calls show a write, then reads; Haiku 4.5 calls are rejected with a 400 error.
Sonnet 5.5 calls show 0 in both fields, and Haiku 4.5 calls write, as the smaller model needs less.
Sonnet 5.5 calls show a write, then reads; Haiku 4.5 calls show 0 in both cache fields and no error.

questions.explanation: The minimum cacheable length is set per model: 512 tokens for Claude Sonnet 5.5 and 4,096 for Claude Haiku 4.5. A 3,000-token prefix clears the first, so Sonnet calls write once and then read. It falls short of the second, so Haiku calls are processed without caching, with no error and both usage fields at 0. Cache entries are also kept per model, so the two tiers cannot share one.

distractor_explanations.A: Cache entries are kept per model, and Haiku 4.5 needs a prefix of at least 4,096 tokens, which 3,000 tokens does not reach.
distractor_explanations.B: A prefix under the minimum is processed without caching and no error is returned. Only the usage fields reveal it.
distractor_explanations.C: The minimum is not lower for the smaller model. Sonnet 5.5 needs 512 tokens and Haiku 4.5 needs 4,096.

questions.prompt: An analysis agent writes a 40,000-token prefix to the cache with the default settings. Its first response streams for 4 minutes 30 seconds. The user replies 45 seconds after the response ends, and the follow-up shows `cache_read_input_tokens: 0` and a fresh cache write. Which change prevents this miss on slow turns?

options.text: Send the first request without streaming and wait for the complete response.
Switch to automatic caching with a top-level `cache_control` field on each request.
Add a second breakpoint on the user's new message in the follow-up.
Set `ttl` to `"1h"` on the breakpoint so the entry outlives long generation times.

questions.explanation: The cache lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, not from the end of its response. A response that streams for 4 minutes 30 seconds leaves only 30 seconds of the default 5 minutes, so a reply 45 seconds later arrives after expiry. A `ttl` of `1h` leaves far more room than any generation time. Analogy: a parking ticket that starts the moment you drive in, not when you walk back from the shops, so a long errand eats the time before you return. A second breakpoint or automatic caching changes where the stamp sits on the ticket, not how long the ticket lasts.

distractor_explanations.A: The lifetime runs from the start of the request in either mode. Streaming does not change when the clock starts.
distractor_explanations.B: Automatic caching only moves the breakpoint to the last cacheable block. The default 5-minute lifetime and the way it is measured stay the same.
distractor_explanations.C: A new breakpoint writes a new entry. It does not extend the life of the earlier entry that already expired.

questions.prompt: A request marks the end of the `tools` array with a 1-hour breakpoint and the latest user message with a 5-minute breakpoint. Which TWO statements about mixing the two lifetimes in one request are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A 1-hour breakpoint must appear earlier in the prompt than any 5-minute breakpoint.
A hit on a 1-hour entry costs more than a hit on a 5-minute entry.
`usage.cache_creation` splits writes into `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` and `ephemeral_5m_input_tokens`.
The 1-hour lifetime is accepted only by the first-party API, and not by Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud.
Tokens read from the cache are billed again at the 5-minute write rate.

questions.explanation: Prompt prefixes are cached in the order tools, system, messages, and each entry covers everything before its breakpoint. Longer-lived entries therefore have to come first, so the 1-hour breakpoint must sit earlier than any 5-minute one. The response reports the split in `usage.cache_creation`, and the two values add up to `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Analogy: a tower of storage boxes where each label stays valid only while everything beneath it is still there, so the longest rentals go at the bottom. The receipt lists month-long and day-long rentals on separate lines. A pricier read on 1-hour entries is the tempting claim, but only the write costs more.

distractor_explanations.B: Hits and refreshes are priced the same for both lifetimes. The 1-hour premium applies only when tokens are written.
distractor_explanations.D: The 1-hour duration is documented as available on the Claude API, Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud and Foundry.
distractor_explanations.E: Tokens up to the highest hit are billed at the read rate. Only the new tokens past that point are charged as writes.

questions.prompt: A team prepares a 50,000-request overnight batch. Every request includes the web search tool and shares one long cached prefix, and nobody needs results before morning. Which TWO statements about this batch are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Cache hits are best-effort, so a `ttl` of `1h` on the shared prefix improves the hit rate.
Processing stops the moment the workspace spend limit is reached, so a batch stays under the cap.
A request may set `stream: true` to receive its tokens as they are generated.
Results stay downloadable for 29 days after the batch finishes processing.
A result may end with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`, and a follow-up request can continue that turn.

Requests are processed concurrently and in any order, so cache hits are best-effort, and a one-hour lifetime on the shared prefix helps entries survive a long run. Analogy: a print shop taking a huge overnight order. Special binding is allowed and a long job may come back half-finished for you to resubmit. The shared master plate is on many presses at once, so reserving it for an hour helps. Live streaming does not exist in that shop.

distractor_explanations.C: `stream` is rejected in batch requests. Results come back together as a single file once processing ends.
distractor_explanations.D: The 29 days count from the batch's creation time, not from when processing ended.

questions.prompt: An agent on Claude Haiku 4.5 uses extended thinking in a tool loop, with one breakpoint on the last block. Reads stay high across every `tool_result` turn. When the user types a new text message, `cache_read_input_tokens` drops sharply and the history is written to the cache again. The same agent on Claude Sonnet 4.6 keeps its reads. What explains the Haiku behavior?

options.text: The prefix fell under the 4,096-token minimum cacheable length for Haiku 4.5.
The new text message changed `tool_choice`, which invalidates the message blocks.
Haiku drops earlier thinking blocks once a typed message arrives, so later messages leave the cache.
Thinking blocks cannot carry `cache_control`, so a turn that contains one is left out of the cache.

questions.explanation: On Haiku models and on earlier Opus and Sonnet models, adding user content that is not a tool result causes earlier thinking blocks to be stripped from context, and the messages after them drop out of the cache. Opus 4.5 and later and Sonnet 4.6 and later keep those blocks, so the prefix stays valid. Analogy: a cook who scribbles notes on an order slip. On older kitchens a new customer request makes the cook bin the earlier notes, and every dish prepared from them is cooked again. Newer kitchens keep the notes. The minimum-length distractor is a real rule, but the history here only grew.

distractor_explanations.A: The minimum is a property of the prompt size, and the history is larger than it was a turn earlier. Nothing shrank below it.
distractor_explanations.B: `tool_choice` did not change here. That setting invalidates message blocks only when its value differs between requests.
distractor_explanations.D: Thinking blocks cannot be marked directly, but they are cached with surrounding content. Reads stayed high across tool-result turns, which shows this is not the cause.

questions.prompt: A report service sends the same 50,000-token prefix once every 20 minutes for three hours, which is nine requests. Assume a base input price of $2 per million tokens, 5-minute writes at 1.25x, 1-hour writes at 2x and cache reads at 0.1x. Counting only the prefix, what does switching the breakpoint from the default lifetime to `ttl: "1h"` do to the cost?

options.text: It cuts the prefix cost by about $0.13, from roughly $1.13 to $1.00.
It cuts the prefix cost by about $1.05, from roughly $1.13 to $0.08.
It raises the prefix cost by about $0.68, from roughly $1.13 to $1.80.
It cuts the prefix cost by about $0.85, from roughly $1.13 to $0.28.

questions.explanation: With the default lifetime, 20 minutes between requests means every request finds the entry expired and pays a 1.25x write: 9 x 50,000 x $2.50 per million is about $1.13. With `1h`, the first request pays a 2x write of about $0.20, and the other eight are reads at 0.1x, about $0.01 each, which keep refreshing the entry. That totals about $0.28, a saving near $0.85. Analogy: single bus tickets versus a day pass. The pass costs more up front, but every later ride is nearly free. The tempting claim that 2x writes always cost more ignores that only one write happens.

distractor_explanations.A: That treats the eight later reads as full-price input. Cache hits are billed at 0.1x, which is $0.20 per million tokens here.
distractor_explanations.B: That figure leaves out the first 1-hour write, which costs 50,000 tokens at 2x, about $0.20.
distractor_explanations.C: That treats every request as a 2x write. After the first write each request is a cheap read that also refreshes the 1-hour entry.

questions.prompt: A first-party API agent puts one `cache_control` breakpoint on the last block of every request. In one turn the model issues 30 parallel `tool_use` blocks and the app returns 30 `tool_result` blocks, so the next request ends more than 60 blocks after the previous breakpoint. What does that request's usage show?

options.text: A read of the earlier entry and no new write; the tool blocks are processed as uncached input.
Earlier entry read, new blocks written; a run of consecutive tool blocks is one lookback position.
A miss unless a second explicit breakpoint is placed within 20 blocks of the first.
A full miss and a new write; the entry is now more than 20 blocks behind the new breakpoint.

questions.explanation: The lookback window checks at most 20 positions per breakpoint, but on the Claude API a run of consecutive `tool_use` blocks counts as one position and so does a run of consecutive `tool_result` blocks. Thirty parallel calls therefore use only a couple of positions, the walk reaches the previous write, and the new blocks are written at the new breakpoint. Analogy: searching a stack of receipts for your last bookmark. A stapled bundle of 30 receipts counts as a single item in the stack. Adding a second breakpoint is the right cure only when real positions pile up past 20.

distractor_explanations.A: With the breakpoint on the last block, the added blocks are written to the cache. They are not left uncached.
distractor_explanations.C: A second breakpoint helps when a growing conversation really adds 20 or more positions. A run of parallel tool blocks does not.
distractor_explanations.D: The 20-position window counts each run of consecutive tool blocks once. Here the earlier entry is only a few positions back.

questions.prompt: A team sends the `diagnostics` object on every turn of a cached conversation. On turn 3, `cache_read_input_tokens` is 0 and the response reports a `cache_miss_reason` of type `tools_changed` with `cache_missed_input_tokens` of 38200. The service builds the `tools` array on each request from a map of schemas. What is the best fix?

Send the tools in a fixed order with deterministically serialized schemas, such as sorted keys.
Keep the history append-only and echo assistant content and tool results back verbatim.

The suggested cure depends on which word is underlined: a changed system prompt, history or model each have their own cure, which are real but belong to other underlines.

distractor_explanations.A: That fixes a `system_changed` result. The report names the `tools` array as the first divergence here.
distractor_explanations.B: That fixes a `model_changed` result. The model is not what differs in this response.
distractor_explanations.D: That fixes a `messages_changed` result, which is reported only when model, system and tools all match.

A request returns a 400 error. The team uses automatic caching and also marks the last block explicitly:

questions.prompt:
A Python Agent SDK service is configured as follows:

```python
async def allow_bash(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    return {"hookSpecificOutput": {
        "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
        "permissionDecision": "allow"}}

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    permission_mode="bypassPermissions",
    disallowed_tools=["Bash(rm *)"],
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="Bash",
                                      hooks=[allow_bash])]},
)
```

Claude proposes `rm -rf build` and then `/bin/rm -rf build`. Which TWO statements are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The `Bash` tool is removed from Claude's context entirely, so neither command is ever attempted.
`rm -rf build` is denied; the hook's `allow` does not skip the deny rule.
Both commands run: a hook's `allow` decision overrides the deny rules.
`/bin/rm -rf build` is not matched by the rule as written and runs under bypass mode.
Both commands are denied; the rule matches commands that invoke `rm` however spelled.

questions.explanation: The SDK checks a tool call in a fixed order: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, the permission mode, allow rules, then the `canUseTool` callback. A hook's `allow` does not skip the deny rules, so `rm -rf build` is blocked even in `bypassPermissions`. A scoped deny such as `Bash(rm *)` matches commands as written and leaves `Bash` available, so `/bin/rm` falls through to a mode that approves it. Analogy: a nightclub with a written ban list. A VIP wristband (the hook) does not erase a name from the list, but the same man under another spelling is not on the list as written, and on open-door night (bypass) he walks in.

distractor_explanations.A: Only a bare name such as `Bash` removes the tool. A scoped rule leaves the tool available and checks each call.
distractor_explanations.C: Hooks run first, but an `allow` from a hook does not skip the deny and ask rules that come after it.
distractor_explanations.E: Scoped rules match commands as written. `/bin/rm` is a different string, so it falls through to the permission mode.

Coordinators that list the agent begin delegating to its new version without being updated.
Fields left out of the update request are reset to their default values on the agent.

A supplied `version` that is not the agent's current version is rejected with a 409.

distractor_explanations.B: A coordinator keeps the version pinned in its roster until the coordinator itself is updated.

questions.prompt: A team tunes prompts for an agent on Claude Sonnet 5.5 with adaptive thinking. Evals show it reasons well on easy tasks but follows a long scripted plan rigidly on hard ones. Which TWO changes fit Anthropic's prompting guidance? (Select TWO.)

questions.prompt: A research agent calls the Messages API with the web search tool set to `max_uses: 3`. The logs show HTTP 200 and `stop_reason: "end_turn"` on every call, yet answers to broad questions are thin. How can the app detect that the limit was reached?

A 400 `invalid_request_error` naming the `max_uses` parameter.
A response with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` that must be sent back to continue.
A `web_search_tool_result` whose `content` is an error object with code `max_uses_exceeded`.

The error appears in the response body as a `web_search_tool_result` whose `content` is a `web_search_tool_result_error` with `error_code` set to `max_uses_exceeded`. Claude sees it and carries on, which explains the thin answers. Analogy: a library card that allows three book requests per visit. The librarian does not call security on the fourth request; she stamps limit reached on the slip, and you leave with what you have. A rate-limit status code is the tempting but different signal.

questions.prompt: A support bot's web search tool must return results only from the vendor's documentation, so the team restricts it with `allowed_domains`. Which TWO statements about how those entries are matched are accurate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: `docs.example.com` returns results only from that subdomain, not from `example.com`.
`example.com` also covers its subdomains, such as `docs.example.com`.
`*.example.com` is the supported wildcard form for covering all subdomains.
`allowed_domains` and `blocked_domains` can be combined, with blocked entries taking priority.
Entries should include the scheme, such as `https://docs.example.com`.

questions.explanation: Domain filters take bare domains without a scheme. A plain domain such as `example.com` also covers its subdomains, while a specific subdomain such as `docs.example.com` restricts results to just that subdomain. Wildcards are accepted only in the path after the domain, and a request that supplies both lists, or an invalid format, is rejected with a 400 `invalid_request_error`. Analogy: a street address. Naming the whole street covers every house on it, while naming house number 12 gets you only that house. A wildcard in front of the street name is something the post office will not accept.

distractor_explanations.C: Wildcards are allowed only in the path after the domain. An entry like `*.example.com` is rejected with a 400.
distractor_explanations.D: Supplying both in one request returns a 400. A request uses one list or the other.
distractor_explanations.E: Entries are bare domains. Including the HTTP or HTTPS scheme makes the format invalid.

questions.prompt: A support agent has `web_fetch` enabled. Its system prompt lists the runbook URL `https://runbooks.example.com/db-failover`, and the user asks it to follow the failover runbook. The tool result is a `web_fetch_tool_result_error` with `error_code` set to `url_not_in_prior_context`. What is the fix?

Add `runbooks.example.com` to `allowed_domains` on the tool.
Set `citations` to `{"enabled": true}` on the tool so the URL is accepted as a source.
Include the URL in a user message, or return it in a client tool result.

A URL that appears only in the system prompt, or only in Claude's own output, is refused with `url_not_in_prior_context`, which limits data exfiltration. Putting the URL in a user message fixes it. Analogy: a courier who collects only from addresses written on a slip a customer hands over. An address pinned on the depot noticeboard does not count, and the depot's approved-areas list is a separate check.

distractor_explanations.A: That setting limits how much fetched content enters context. The fetch here was refused before any content was read.
distractor_explanations.B: Domain filtering produces `url_not_allowed`. This error says the URL never appeared in the conversation.
distractor_explanations.C: Citations control whether the answer cites passages. They do not decide which URLs may be fetched.

questions.prompt: An agent built with the SDK tool runner is about to get a `refund_order` tool. Company policy requires a person to approve every refund before it executes, and refunds must never run unattended. Which approach fits?

Keep the tool runner and set `max_iterations` to 1 so the loop stops before each refund.

distractor_explanations.C: By then the refunds have already run. A review of the final message comes too late.

A noticeboard asking visitors to behave is not a lock.

distractor_explanations.A: A deny list blocks only the hosts it names. Any unlisted host would still be allowed without a prompt in bypass mode.
distractor_explanations.B: `strictAllowlist` set in a repository's settings has no effect. It is read from user, managed or command-line settings.

questions.prompt: A team adds `Write(./infra/**)` to `permissions.deny` to stop file changes under `infra/`, while Claude must still be able to read those files. Afterwards Claude edits `infra/main.tf` with its Edit tool. What is the correct fix?

questions.prompt: A developer is deep in a long Claude Code session where `Allow for this session` approvals for `npm test` and `git diff` are already granted. They want to try a different design on a copy of the conversation, leave the original session untouched on disk, and keep those approvals without granting them again. Which action fits best?

Run `/clear`, then describe the design to Claude again from scratch
Run `/branch try-streaming` from inside the session that is already running
Exit the session, then start a new process with `claude --continue --fork-session`

distractor_explanations.B: `/clear` saves the old conversation but starts the new one empty, so there is no copy of the conversation to work from.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Exam-Style Tier)
questions.prompt: A support agent has been live for a month. The team keeps a 40-task capability eval that the agent passes about half the time. Customers have reported 25 distinct failures in the support queue, and engineers fix them one at a time, worried that earlier fixes will break. What is the best addition to the eval work?

Turn each reported failure into a task with a clear pass/fail check and run them on every change

Each should be unambiguous, so that two experts would reach the same verdict, and be graded by a check that can run on every change. Held apart from capability evals, which start with low pass rates, these form a regression suite expected to pass nearly every time. Analogy: a mechanic's logbook. Mixing the list in with experimental road tests would blur what the score means.

distractor_explanations.B: The guidance is to start with 20-50 tasks drawn from real failures, since early gains are large. Waiting delays protection against regressions.
